# futures_timer - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/futures-timer/

## Expand description

A general purpose crate for working with timeouts and delays with futures.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use std::time::Duration;
use futures_timer::Delay;
let now = Delay::new(Duration::from_secs(3)).await;
println!("waited for 3 secs");
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Delay](https://docs.rs/struct.Delay.html)
- A future representing the notification that an elapsed duration has occurred.

# async_std - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/async-std/^1.13/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#async-std-has-been-discontinued-use-smol-instead)`async-std` has been discontinued; use `smol` instead

We created `async-std` to demonstrate the value of making a library as close to
`std` as possible, but async. We think that demonstration was successful, and
we hope it will influence future design and development directions of async in
`std`. However, in the meantime, the [ smol](https://github.com/smol-rs/smol/)
project came about and provided a great executor and libraries for asynchronous
use in the Rust ecosystem. We think that resources would be better spent
consolidating around

`smol`, rather than continuing to provide occasional
maintenance of `async-std`. As such, we recommend that all users of
`async-std`, and all libraries built on `async-std`, switch to `smol` instead.In addition to the `smol` project as a direct replacement, you may find other
parts of the futures ecosystem useful, including `futures-concurrency`,
`async-io`, `futures-lite`, and `async-compat`.

[§](https://docs.rs#async-version-of-the-rust-standard-library)Async version of the Rust standard library

`async-std` is a foundation of portable Rust software, a set of minimal and battle-tested
shared abstractions for the [broader Rust ecosystem](https://crates.io). It offers std types, like
[ Future](https://docs.rs/future/trait.Future.html) and

[, library-defined](https://docs.rs/stream/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream`[operations on language primitives](https://docs.rs#primitives),

[standard macros](https://docs.rs#macros),

[I/O](https://docs.rs/io/index.html)and

[multithreading](https://docs.rs/task/index.html), among

[many other things](https://docs.rs#what-is-in-the-standard-library-documentation).

`async-std` is available from [crates.io](https://crates.io). Once included, `async-std` can be accessed
in [ use](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch07-02-defining-modules-to-control-scope-and-privacy.html) statements through the path

`async_std`, as in [.](https://docs.rs/future/index.html)

`use async_std::future`[§](https://docs.rs#how-to-read-this-documentation)How to read this documentation

If you already know the name of what you are looking for, the fastest way to
find it is to use the [search
bar](https://docs.rs) at the top of the page.

Otherwise, you may want to jump to one of these useful sections:

If this is your first time, the documentation for `async-std` is
written to be casually perused. Clicking on interesting things should
generally lead you to interesting places. Still, there are important bits
you don’t want to miss, so read on for a tour of the `async-std` and
its documentation!

Once you are familiar with the contents of `async-std` you may
begin to find the verbosity of the prose distracting. At this stage in your
development you may want to press the `[-]` button near the top of the
page to collapse it into a more skimmable view.

While you are looking at that `[-]` button also notice the `[src]`
button. Rust’s API documentation comes with the source code and you are
encouraged to read it. The `async-std` source is generally high
quality and a peek behind the curtains is often enlightening.

Modules in this crate are organized in the same way as in `std`, except blocking
functions have been replaced with async functions and threads have been replaced with
lightweight tasks.

You can find more information, reading materials, and other resources here:

[§](https://docs.rs#what-is-in-the-async-std-documentation)What is in the `async-std` documentation?

First, `async-std` is divided into a number of focused
modules, [all listed further down this page](https://docs.rs#modules). These modules are
the bedrock upon which async Rust is forged, and they have mighty names
like [ async_std::os](https://docs.rs/os/index.html) and

[. Modules’ documentation typically includes an overview of the module along with examples, and are a smart place to start familiarizing yourself with the library.](https://docs.rs/task/index.html)

`async_std::task`Second, `async-std` defines [The Async Prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html), a small collection
of items - mostly traits - that should be imported into every module of
every async crate. The traits in the prelude are pervasive, making the
prelude documentation a good entry point to learning about the library.

And finally, `async-std` exports a number of async macros, and
[lists them on this page](https://docs.rs#macros).

[§](https://docs.rs#contributing-changes-to-the-documentation)Contributing changes to the documentation

Check out `async-std`’s contribution guidelines [here](https://async.rs/contribute).
The source for this documentation can be found on [GitHub](https://github.com/async-rs).
To contribute changes, make sure you read the guidelines first, then submit
pull requests for your suggested changes.

Contributions are appreciated! If you see a part of the docs that can be
improved, submit a PR, or chat with us first on
[Discord](https://discord.gg/JvZeVNe).

[§](https://docs.rs#a-tour-of-async-std)A tour of `async-std`

The rest of this crate documentation is dedicated to pointing out notable
features of `async-std`.

[§](https://docs.rs#platform-abstractions-and-io)Platform abstractions and I/O

Besides basic data types, `async-std` is largely concerned with
abstracting over differences in common platforms, most notably Windows and
Unix derivatives.

Common types of I/O, including [files](https://docs.rs/fs/struct.File.html), [TCP](https://docs.rs/net/struct.TcpStream.html), [UDP](https://docs.rs/net/struct.UdpSocket.html), are defined in the
[ io](https://docs.rs/io/index.html),

[, and](https://docs.rs/fs/index.html)

`fs`[modules.](https://docs.rs/net/index.html)

`net`The [ task](https://docs.rs/task/index.html) module contains

`async-std`’s task abstractions. [contains further primitive shared memory types.](https://docs.rs/sync/index.html)

`sync`[contains the channel types for message passing.](https://docs.rs/channel/index.html)

`channel`[§](https://docs.rs#timeouts-intervals-and-delays)Timeouts, intervals, and delays

`async-std` provides several methods to manipulate time:

- `task::sleep`
- `stream::interval`
- `future::timeout`

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

All examples require the [ "attributes" feature](https://docs.rs#features) to be enabled.
This feature is not enabled by default because it significantly impacts
compile times. See

[for an alternative way to start executing tasks.](https://docs.rs/task/fn.block_on.html)

`task::block_on`Call an async function from the main function:

```
async fn say_hello() {
    println!("Hello, world!");
}
#[async_std::main]
async fn main() {
    say_hello().await;
}
```
Await two futures concurrently, and return a tuple of their output:

```
use async_std::prelude::*;
#[async_std::main]
async fn main() {
    let a = async { 1u8 };
    let b = async { 2u8 };
    assert_eq!(a.join(b).await, (1u8, 2u8))
}
```
Create a UDP server that echoes back each received message to the sender:

```
use async_std::net::UdpSocket;
#[async_std::main]
async fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
    let socket = UdpSocket::bind("127.0.0.1:8080").await?;
    println!("Listening on {}", socket.local_addr()?);
    let mut buf = vec![0u8; 1024];
    loop {
        let (recv, peer) = socket.recv_from(&mut buf).await?;
        let sent = socket.send_to(&buf[..recv], &peer).await?;
        println!("Sent {} out of {} bytes to {}", sent, recv, peer);
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

Items marked with <span class=“module-item stab portability” style=“display: inline; border-radius: 3px; padding: 2px; font-size: 80%; line-height: 1.2;”

`unstable`are available only when the`unstable`Cargo feature is enabled:

```
[dependencies.async-std]
version = "1.7.0"
features = ["unstable"]
```
Items marked with <span class=“module-item stab portability” style=“display: inline; border-radius: 3px; padding: 2px; font-size: 80%; line-height: 1.2;”

`attributes`are available only when the`attributes`Cargo feature is enabled:

```
[dependencies.async-std]
version = "1.7.0"
features = ["attributes"]
```
Compatibility with the `tokio` 1.0 runtime is also simultaneously possible
using the `tokio1` Cargo feature:

```
[dependencies.async-std]
version = "1.7.0"
features = ["tokio1"]
```
Compatibility with the `tokio` 0.2 runtime is possible using the `tokio02`
Cargo feature:

```
[dependencies.async-std]
version = "1.7.0"
features = ["tokio02"]
```
Compatibility with the `tokio` 0.3 runtime is also simultaneously possible
using the `tokio03` Cargo feature:

```
[dependencies.async-std]
version = "1.7.0"
features = ["tokio03"]
```
Additionally it’s possible to only use the core traits and combinators by
only enabling the `std` Cargo feature:

```
[dependencies.async-std]
version = "1.7.0"
default-features = false
features = ["std"]
```
And to use async-std on `no_std` targets that only support `alloc` only
enable the `alloc` Cargo feature:

```
[dependencies.async-std]
version = "1.7.0"
default-features = false
features = ["alloc"]
```
[§](https://docs.rs#runtime-configuration)Runtime configuration

Several environment variables are available to tune the async-std runtime:

- `ASYNC_STD_THREAD_COUNT`: The number of threads that the async-std runtime will start. By default, this is one per logical cpu as determined by- [async-global-executor](https://docs.rs/async-global-executor/2.4.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/async_global_executor/index.html), which may be different than the number of physical cpus. Async-std- *will panic*if this is set to any value other than a positive integer.
- `ASYNC_STD_THREAD_NAME`: The name that async-std’s runtime threads report to the operating system. The default value is- `"async-std/runtime"`.

# futures - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/futures/^0.3.1/

## Expand description

Abstractions for asynchronous programming.

This crate provides a number of core abstractions for writing asynchronous code:

- [Futures](https://docs.rs/future/index.html)are single eventual values produced by asynchronous computations. Some programming languages (e.g. JavaScript) call this concept “promise”.
- [Streams](https://docs.rs/stream/index.html)represent a series of values produced asynchronously.
- [Sinks](https://docs.rs/sink/index.html)provide support for asynchronous writing of data.
- [Executors](https://docs.rs/executor/index.html)are responsible for running asynchronous tasks.

The crate also contains abstractions for [asynchronous I/O](https://docs.rs/io/index.html) and
[cross-task communication](https://docs.rs/channel/index.html).

Underlying all of this is the *task system*, which is a form of lightweight
threading. Large asynchronous computations are built up using futures,
streams and sinks, and then spawned as independent tasks that are run to
completion, but *do not block* the thread running them.

The following example describes how the task system context is built and used within macros and keywords such as async and await!.

```
fn main() {
    let pool = ThreadPool::new().expect("Failed to build pool");
    let (tx, rx) = mpsc::unbounded::<i32>();
    // Create a future by an async block, where async is responsible for an
    // implementation of Future. At this point no executor has been provided
    // to this future, so it will not be running.
    let fut_values = async {
        // Create another async block, again where the Future implementation
        // is generated by async. Since this is inside of a parent async block,
        // it will be provided with the executor of the parent block when the parent
        // block is executed.
        //
        // This executor chaining is done by Future::poll whose second argument
        // is a std::task::Context. This represents our executor, and the Future
        // implemented by this async block can be polled using the parent async
        // block's executor.
        let fut_tx_result = async move {
            (0..100).for_each(|v| {
                tx.unbounded_send(v).expect("Failed to send");
            })
        };
        // Use the provided thread pool to spawn the generated future
        // responsible for transmission
        pool.spawn_ok(fut_tx_result);
        let fut_values = rx
            .map(|v| v * 2)
            .collect();
        // Use the executor provided to this async block to wait for the
        // future to complete.
        fut_values.await
    };
    // Actually execute the above future, which will invoke Future::poll and
    // subsequently chain appropriate Future::poll and methods needing executors
    // to drive all futures. Eventually fut_values will be driven to completion.
    let values: Vec<i32> = executor::block_on(fut_values);
    println!("Values={:?}", values);
}
```
The majority of examples and code snippets in this crate assume that they are inside an async block as written above.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [join](https://docs.rs/macro.join.html)- `async-await`
- Polls multiple futures simultaneously, returning a tuple of all results once complete.
- [pending](https://docs.rs/macro.pending.html)- `async-await`
- A macro which yields to the event loop once.
- [pin_mut](https://docs.rs/macro.pin_mut.html)
- Pins a value on the stack.
- [poll](https://docs.rs/macro.poll.html)- `async-await`
- A macro which returns the result of polling a future once within the
current `async`context.
- [ready](https://docs.rs/macro.ready.html)
- Extracts the successful type of `Poll<T>`.
- [select](https://docs.rs/macro.select.html)- `async-await`and- `std`
- Polls multiple futures and streams simultaneously, executing the branch
for the future that finishes first. If multiple futures are ready,
one will be pseudo-randomly selected at runtime. Futures directly
passed to `select!`must be`Unpin`and implement`FusedFuture`.
- [select_](https://docs.rs/macro.select_biased.html)- biased - `async-await`
- Polls multiple futures and streams simultaneously, executing the branch
for the future that finishes first. Unlike `select!``select_biased!`must be`Unpin`and implement`FusedFuture`.
- [stream_](https://docs.rs/macro.stream_select.html)- select - `async-await`and- `std`
- Combines several streams, all producing the same `Item`type, into one stream. This is similar to`select_all`but does not require the streams to all be the same type. It also keeps the streams inline, and does not require`Box<dyn Stream>`s to be allocated. Streams passed to this macro must be`Unpin`.
- [try_](https://docs.rs/macro.try_join.html)- join - `async-await`
- Polls multiple futures simultaneously, resolving to a `Result`

# gloo_timers - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/gloo-timers/^0.4.0/

## Expand description

Working with timers on the Web: `setTimeout` and `setInterval`.

These APIs come in two flavors:

- a callback style (that more directly mimics the JavaScript APIs), and
- a `Future`s and`Stream`s API.

[§](https://docs.rs#timeouts)Timeouts

Timeouts fire once after a period of time (measured in milliseconds).

[§](https://docs.rs#timeouts-with-a-callback-function)Timeouts with a Callback Function

```
use gloo_timers::callback::Timeout;
let timeout = Timeout::new(1_000, move || {
    // Do something after the one second timeout is up!
});
// Since we don't plan on cancelling the timeout, call `forget`.
timeout.forget();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#timeouts-as-futures)Timeouts as `Future`s

With the `futures` feature enabled, a `future` module containing futures-based
timers is exposed.

```
use gloo_timers::future::TimeoutFuture;
use wasm_bindgen_futures::spawn_local;
// Spawn the `timeout` future on the local thread. If we just dropped it, then
// the timeout would be cancelled with `clearTimeout`.
spawn_local(async {
    TimeoutFuture::new(1_000).await;
    // Do something here after the one second timeout is up!
});
```
[§](https://docs.rs#intervals)Intervals

Intervals fire repeatedly every *n* milliseconds.

[§](https://docs.rs#intervals-with-a-callback-function)Intervals with a Callback Function

# send_wrapper - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/send_wrapper/^0.6.0/

## Expand description

This [Rust](https://www.rust-lang.org) library implements a wrapper type called [ SendWrapper](https://docs.rs/struct.SendWrapper.html) which allows you to move around non-

[types between threads, as long as you access the contained value only from within the original thread. You also have to make sure that the wrapper is dropped from within the original thread. If any of these constraints is violated, a panic occurs.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Send.html)

`Send`[implements](https://docs.rs/struct.SendWrapper.html)

`SendWrapper<T>`[and](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Send.html)

`Send`[for any type](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sync.html)

`Sync``T`.The idea for this library was born in the context of a [ GTK+](https://www.gtk.org/)/

[-based application.](http://gtk-rs.org/)

`gtk-rs`[applications are strictly single-threaded. It is not allowed to call any](https://www.gtk.org/)

`GTK+`[method from a thread different to the main thread. Consequently, all](https://www.gtk.org/)

`GTK+`[structs are non-](http://gtk-rs.org/)

`gtk-rs`[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Send.html)

`Send`Sometimes you still want to do some work in background. It is possible to enqueue [ GTK+](https://www.gtk.org/) calls from there to be
executed in the main thread

[using](http://gtk-rs.org/docs/glib/source/fn.idle_add.html). This way you can know, that the

`Glib`[structs involved are only accessed in the main thread and will also be dropped there. This library makes it possible that](http://gtk-rs.org/)

`gtk-rs`[structs can leave the main thread at all.](http://gtk-rs.org/)

`gtk-rs`[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use send_wrapper::SendWrapper;
use std::rc::Rc;
use std::thread;
use std::sync::mpsc::channel;
// This import is important if you want to use deref() or
// deref_mut() instead of Deref coercion.
use std::ops::{Deref, DerefMut};
// Rc is a non-Send type.
let value = Rc::new(42);
// We now wrap the value with `SendWrapper` (value is moved inside).
let wrapped_value = SendWrapper::new(value);
// A channel allows us to move the wrapped value between threads.
let (sender, receiver) = channel();
let t = thread::spawn(move || {
    // This would panic (because of dereferencing in wrong thread):
    // let value = wrapped_value.deref();
	// Move SendWrapper back to main thread, so it can be dropped from there.
	// If you leave this out the thread will panic because of dropping from wrong thread.
	sender.send(wrapped_value).unwrap();
});
let wrapped_value = receiver.recv().unwrap();
// Now you can use the value again.
let value = wrapped_value.deref();
// alternatives for dereferencing:
let value = &*wrapped_value;
let value: &Rc<_> = &wrapped_value;
let mut wrapped_value = wrapped_value;
// alternatives for mutable dereferencing:
let value = wrapped_value.deref_mut();
let value = &mut *wrapped_value;
let value: &mut Rc<_> = &mut wrapped_value;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

This crate has a single feature called `futures` that enables [ Future](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/future/future/trait.Future.html) and

[implementations for](https://docs.rs/futures-core/0.3.32/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/futures_core/stream/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream`[. You can enable it in](https://docs.rs/struct.SendWrapper.html)

`SendWrapper``Cargo.toml` like so:`send_wrapper = { version = "...", features = ["futures"] }`[§](https://docs.rs#license)License

`send_wrapper` is distributed under the terms of both the MIT license and the Apache License (Version 2.0).

See LICENSE-APACHE.txt, and LICENSE-MIT.txt for details.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Send](https://docs.rs/struct.SendWrapper.html)- Wrapper
- A wrapper which allows you to move around non-`Send`

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (4c9d2bfe4 2026-07-01)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# gdscript_scene - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/gdscript-scene/0.5.4/gdscript_scene/

## Expand description

`gdscript-scene` — a `.tscn`/`.tres` **text** parser for scene-aware analysis (Phase 4).

Internal layer (not a stable API).Depend on[(the public surface); the items here may change between releases.](https://docs.rs/gdscript-ide)`gdscript-ide`

Godot’s text scene format is INI-like: bracketed section headers (`[node …]`, `[ext_resource …]`,
…) followed by `key = value` property lines. This crate parses that structure — node names,
types, parent paths, attached scripts, `unique_name_in_owner`, and instanced sub-scenes — into a
`SceneModel`**with byte spans**, so the type layer (Phase-4 M1+) can resolve `$Path` /
`%Unique` / `get_node("…")` to a node’s real `Control`/`Node` subclass instead of bare `Node` —
intelligence the Godot editor’s own LSP produces only in-editor and never flows into inference.

**M0 scope:** the pure, wasm-clean [ parse_scene](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_scene.html) (

`&str -> SceneModel`) + the model + byte
spans. It **records**the typing inputs (

`type=`/`script=`/`instance=`); it does **not**resolve a

`Ty` (M1), recurse into instanced sub-scenes, build the project-wide script↔scene index, or
cache via salsa (M1+). See `plans/PHASE-4-M0-PLAYBOOK.md`.**Invariant:** the parser is strictly additive and **never fails** — every binary/malformed/
unknown form degrades to an empty-or-partial model + a [ SceneProblem](https://docs.rs/enum.SceneProblem.html), never a panic or

`Err`.
The floor is always parity with the engine’s `Node`-everywhere baseline.**Portability:** a core crate — wasm32-clean (no `std::fs`, no `Instant`, no threads); `.tscn`
text is injected via the VFS exactly like `.gd`.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [ExtId](https://docs.rs/struct.ExtId.html)
- An `ext_resource`/`sub_resource`id — the opaque, quoted-string key as written (`"1"`,`"1_app"`,`"StyleBoxFlat_x"`). A 3.x bare-int id is normalized to its string form.
- [ExtResource](https://docs.rs/struct.ExtResource.html)
- An `[ext_resource …]`declaration.
- [NodeIdx](https://docs.rs/struct.NodeIdx.html)
- Index of a node into `SceneModel::nodes`
- [Node](https://docs.rs/struct.NodeProp.html)- Prop
- One body property line of a `[node …]`—`key = value`(value skipped). The key may be a bare identifier (an`@export`var or an engine property) or a`group/sub`override path.
- [Scene](https://docs.rs/struct.SceneConnection.html)- Connection
- One `[connection …]`section — a signal wired to a method in the editor. The four spans are the**inner identifier**byte ranges (surrounding quotes excluded), so a rename rewrites exactly the name. A connection has no body.
- [Scene](https://docs.rs/struct.SceneModel.html)- Model
- One parsed `.tscn`/`.tres`. Produced by`crate::parse_scene`**never**an`Err`— every malformed/binary/unknown form degrades to an empty-or-partial model plus a`SceneProblem``PartialEq`/`Eq`so it can be a backdated salsa query result (`Arc<SceneModel>`) in M1.
- [Scene](https://docs.rs/struct.SceneNode.html)- Node
- One `[node …]`section: its header attributes + the two body properties we read.
- [SubResource](https://docs.rs/struct.SubResource.html)
- A `[sub_resource …]`declaration (type only — the value body is skipped).

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Node](https://docs.rs/enum.NodePathResolution.html)- Path - Resolution
- The reason a node path did (not) resolve — for the `INVALID_NODE_PATH`decision (M2).
- [Scene](https://docs.rs/enum.SceneKind.html)- Kind
- Whether the parsed file is a `.tscn`scene (`gd_scene`) or a`.tres`resource (`gd_resource`).
- [Scene](https://docs.rs/enum.SceneProblem.html)- Problem
- A non-fatal problem found during parsing. The parser records these and keeps going — the floor
is always parity with the engine’s `Node`-everywhere baseline.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_scene.html)- scene
- Parse `.tscn`/`.tres`text into a`SceneModel``Err`.

# gdscript_db - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/gdscript-db/0.5.4/gdscript_db/

## Expand description

`gdscript-db` — the input layer for the analyzer.

Internal layer (not a stable API).Depend on[(the public surface); the items here may change between releases.](https://docs.rs/gdscript-ide)`gdscript-ide`

Holds the virtual file system (`FileId` → text, always injected — never `std::fs`), the
project model, and (from Phase 3) the **salsa** query graph: `#[salsa::input]`s set via
`apply_change`, `#[salsa::tracked]` derived queries, durability tiers. The Phase-0/1/2
plain VFS map + reparse-on-change is being replaced here, localized behind the unchanged
`gdscript-ide` public API (Playbook §3.M0).

Crate boundary: `gdscript-db` is the *base* of the salsa stack — it owns the [ Db](https://docs.rs/trait.Db.html) trait,
the inputs, and the

[query (it may depend on](https://docs.rs/fn.parse.html)

`parse``gdscript-syntax`, never on
`gdscript-hir`). The higher queries (`item_tree`, `analyze_file`) live in `gdscript-hir`,
which depends on this crate for `&dyn Db`. This one-way layering is what avoids a
`db ↔ hir` dependency cycle.`FileId` is deliberately **not** a salsa input. The `FileId → FileText` mapping is a side
table ([ Files](https://docs.rs/struct.Files.html)) the database owns, mirroring rust-analyzer’s

`base-db`: `FileId`s are
assigned by the client/loader and stay opaque ids, while the salsa input is the *text*.

Must build for `wasm32` (single-threaded; salsa with `default-features = false`).

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Engine](https://docs.rs/struct.EngineGeneration.html)- Generation
- A generation counter that makes the otherwise-untracked runtime engine model **invalidate**correctly. The engine model is a leaked`&'static`side handle (not a salsa input), so a query memoized while it was still absent (`engine() == None`, on`wasm32`before`set_engine_api`) would otherwise return that stale empty result forever. Every`engine()`read records a dependency on this input;`set_engine_api`bumps it, recomputing those queries. The*value*is irrelevant — only that setting it advances the revision. Used on`wasm32`only (native has the bundled model from the start, so it never changes — no generation tracking, no overhead).
- [File](https://docs.rs/struct.FileText.html)- Text
- The VFS leaf: one file’s UTF-8 text, as a salsa input, plus its `FileId``FileText`can recover the id for cross-file resolution) and its`res://`path (so`preload`/`extends "res://…"`resolve to the declaring file — M3).
- [Files](https://docs.rs/struct.Files.html)
- The `FileId → FileText`side table.`Arc`-backed so a cheap clone shares the same map — needed to mutate an input (`&mut dyn Db`) without simultaneously borrowing`self.files`.
- [Project](https://docs.rs/struct.ProjectConfig.html)- Config
- The project’s `project.godot`, injected as raw text — the wasm-clean core never reads the filesystem, so the loader pushes the bytes exactly like a`.gd`file. The autoload index is a tracked query that parses this text (M4). Held at`MEDIUM`durability (project structure, stable across`.gd`keystrokes), so a body edit (LOW) never invalidates the autoload registry.
- [Root](https://docs.rs/struct.RootDatabase.html)- Database
- The concrete analyzer database — a salsa `Storage`plus the`Files`
- [Source](https://docs.rs/struct.SourceRoot.html)- Root
- The project’s file set — a salsa input so project-wide queries (the global `class_name`registry, M1) iterate the files incrementally. It changes only when a file is**added or removed**, never on a body edit, and is held at MEDIUM durability — so a keystroke (a`LOW`change) never invalidates project-wide derived data.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Warning](https://docs.rs/enum.WarningOverride.html)- Override
- The database trait `gdscript-hir`/`gdscript-ide`depend on.`#[salsa::db]`on the*trait*makes it a salsa supertrait, so any`&dyn Db`upcasts to`&dyn salsa::Database`and every`#[salsa::tracked]`free function downstream can take`db: &dyn Db`. A host/CLI-level override of the warning-strictness baseline`type_diagnostics`resolves against (regardless of`project.godot`presence). A plain (non-salsa) per-session policy knob: it is read**only**inside the non-tracked`type_diagnostics`, so it never enters the salsa query graph and cannot break the W1 firewall (a warning-level change must never re-run inference).

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [parse](https://docs.rs/fn.parse.html)
- Parse a file to its lossless CST. Memoized; re-parses only when the file text changes.

# gdscript_fmt - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/gdscript-fmt/0.5.4/gdscript_fmt/

## Expand description

`gdscript-fmt` — the GDScript source formatter (Phase-6 Workstream 3).

Internal layer (not a stable API).Depend on[(the public surface); the items here may change between releases.](https://docs.rs/gdscript-ide)`gdscript-ide`

A pure `fn(source, &FmtConfig) -> String`: no engine model, no filesystem, `wasm32`-safe.
It re-emits the lexer/pre-pass token stream, normalizing **block indentation** (to the
configured unit), **trailing whitespace**, and the **final newline** — every *significant*
token (keywords, identifiers, literals — including multi-line strings, which are single tokens)
is emitted **verbatim**, so meaning cannot change.

It also normalizes **intra-line spacing** (Phase-4 increment A): one space around binary
operators / assignments / `->` / `:=`, after `,` and `:` (in type-annotation and dict contexts),
hugged brackets (`f(x, y)`, `[1, 2]`), tight member access (`a.b`), and tight unary `-x`. The
decision is purely local (previous significant token + innermost bracket), and the genuinely
ambiguous contexts — slice colons `arr[a:b]`, and node-path sigils `$Node/Path` / `%Unique`
(where a stray space around `/` would silently change meaning **without** changing the token
sequence) — are left **verbatim** / kept tight by a small node-path state machine.

**Safe by construction.** In `safe_mode` (the default) the formatter (a) refuses to touch a
file with syntax errors, and (b) re-lexes its own output and **falls back to the original** if
the significant token sequence changed. So it never corrupts code, even input it doesn’t fully
understand. The result is idempotent: `format(format(x)) == format(x)`.

It also performs **length-driven line reflow** (Phase-4 increment C): a single-line statement
that exceeds `line_width` and contains a bracketed group is wrapped flat → compact → exploded via
a small `Doc`-IR, matching gdformat and preserving the token sequence. The remaining gdformat
behaviours (magic trailing comma, operator-chain paren injection, quote normalization) are
token-mutating and documented in `DEVIATIONS.md`.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [FmtConfig](https://docs.rs/struct.FmtConfig.html)
- Formatter options. Defaults match the Godot convention (tabs) and keep the safety net on.
- [Range](https://docs.rs/struct.RangeEdit.html)- Edit
- A single whole-line replacement edit produced by `format_range`

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [format](https://docs.rs/fn.format.html)
- Format `source`, returning the tidied text. In`safe_mode`(the default) this returns`source`unchanged rather than risk a meaning-changing edit (a syntax error in the input, or output whose significant tokens differ from the input’s).
- [format_](https://docs.rs/fn.format_range.html)- range
- Format only the part of `source`overlapping the byte range`sel`(for editor “format selection” / LSP`textDocument/rangeFormatting`). The whole document is formatted for correct structure and indentation; the result is the**minimal changed line-hunk**that intersects`sel`, or`None`if nothing in the selection’s lines changes. Applying the edit yields the same bytes the whole-file [`format`] would have produced for that region.

# gdscript_syntax - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/gdscript-syntax/0.5.4/gdscript_syntax/

## Expand description

`gdscript-syntax` — lexer + indentation pre-pass + lossless parser for GDScript.

Internal layer (not a stable API).Depend on[(the public surface); the items here may change between releases.](https://docs.rs/gdscript-ide)`gdscript-ide`

Phase 1 fills this in: a `logos` lexer, a hand-written indentation pre-pass
(INDENT/DEDENT/NEWLINE), and a hand-written recursive-descent parser producing a
lossless [ cstree](https://docs.rs/cstree/0.14.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/cstree/index.html) CST plus a typed AST, behind a

`Parser` trait
(tree-sitter-gdscript is the differential test oracle, never the
grammar-of-record — see ADR-0002).The crate “knows nothing about salsa or LSP” (rust-analyzer’s `syntax` layer):
it is pure text → tree. It must build for `wasm32` — no `std::fs`, no clocks, no
threads.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [ast](https://docs.rs/ast/index.html)
- WS4 — the typed AST.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Indent](https://docs.rs/struct.IndentDiagnostic.html)- Diagnostic
- An indentation diagnostic produced while injecting block-structure markers.
Byte-ranged; mapped into a `gdscript-base``Diagnostic`by the IDE layer.
- [Parse](https://docs.rs/struct.Parse.html)
- The result of parsing a source file: a lossless green tree, the interner needed to read token text back, and the diagnostics gathered while parsing.
- [RawToken](https://docs.rs/struct.RawToken.html)
- A lexed token: its `SyntaxKind`
- [Syntax](https://docs.rs/struct.SyntaxError.html)- Error
- A byte-ranged syntax diagnostic with an “expected X” style message.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Syntax](https://docs.rs/enum.SyntaxKind.html)- Kind
- Every terminal and non-terminal kind in the GDScript syntax tree.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [parse](https://docs.rs/fn.parse.html)
- Parse GDScript source into a lossless `Parse`
- [run_](https://docs.rs/fn.run_prepass.html)- prepass
- Inject `Newline`/`Indent`/`Dedent`markers into the lexer token stream.
- [tokenize](https://docs.rs/fn.tokenize.html)
- Lex `src`into a lossless`RawToken``SyntaxKind::Error`

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [GdNode](https://docs.rs/type.GdNode.html)
- A resolved (interner-carrying) red node — supports `Display`/`.text()`and the byte-exact round-trip. This is the public tree type for callers that need text.
- [GdToken](https://docs.rs/type.GdToken.html)
- A resolved red token.
- [Syntax](https://docs.rs/type.SyntaxNode.html)- Node
- A bare (resolver-less) red node — cheap, `Send + Sync`; text needs a resolver.

# gdscript_api - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/gdscript-api/0.5.4/gdscript_api/

## Expand description

`gdscript-api` — the Godot engine model, generated from `extension_api.json`.

Internal layer (not a stable API).Depend on[(the public surface); the items here may change between releases.](https://docs.rs/gdscript-ide)`gdscript-ide`

The model (engine classes + inheritance chain, methods, properties, signals, enums,
constants, singletons, utility functions, builtin Variant types) plus the hand-authored
GDScript layer the dump omits (pseudo-constants + builtin functions). See
`plans/PHASE-2-IMPLEMENTATION-PLAYBOOK.md` §4.

[§](https://docs.rs#shape)Shape

[ model::ApiData](https://docs.rs/model/struct.ApiData.html) is the serializable root that

`xtask codegen-api` `rkyv`-encodes into a
binary blob; [deserializes it once, rebuilds the name indices, merges the hand-authored layer, and exposes the lookup API (](https://docs.rs/struct.EngineApi.html)

`EngineApi``lookup.rs`). The model is `Arc`-shared
and excluded from per-file timing, so the one-time deserialize is amortized.[§](https://docs.rs#targets)Targets

Native builds embed the blob via `include_bytes!` ([ bundled](https://docs.rs/fn.bundled.html), behind the default

`bundled-api` feature). The crate never touches `std::fs`/clocks/threads, so it builds for
`wasm32`; there the blob is **not**embedded (Playbook §4.5) — the host fetches it and calls

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.EngineApi.html#method.from_bytes)

`EngineApi::from_bytes`## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

# gdscript_base - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/gdscript-base/0.5.4/gdscript_base/

## Expand description

`gdscript-base` — foundational POD types shared across the gdscript-analyzer.

The lowest layer of the crate stack (`plans/01-ARCHITECTURE.md` §1). It holds the
engine-/protocol-neutral, `serde`-serializable result structs every client maps to
its own protocol, plus byte-offset position types and a [ LineIndex](https://docs.rs/struct.LineIndex.html) for the
byte↔(line, column) and byte↔UTF-16 conversions LSP clients need.

All offsets are **byte** offsets into a file’s UTF-8 source. No logic beyond the
conversions lives here. The crate is `wasm32`-safe (no `std::fs`, clocks, threads).

These POD result structs are the analyzer’s **public wire contract** (consumed via
[ gdscript_ide](https://docs.rs/gdscript-ide)), so every public item is documented and

`#![deny(missing_docs)]` keeps it that way.## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [semantic_](https://docs.rs/semantic_token_modifier/index.html)- token_ - modifier
- Bit flags for `SemanticToken::modifiers`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Cancelled](https://docs.rs/struct.Cancelled.html)
- A read query was cancelled by a concurrent change. (Phase 1 never actually cancels, but the type is on the API surface so the Phase 3 salsa swap is source-compatible.)
- [Code](https://docs.rs/struct.CodeAction.html)- Action
- A code action / quick-fix: a titled, optionally-kinded `SourceChange`
- [Completion](https://docs.rs/struct.CompletionItem.html)- Item
- A by-name completion suggestion.
- [Diagnostic](https://docs.rs/struct.Diagnostic.html)
- A diagnostic with a byte range, a stable machine code, a severity, and a message.
- [Document](https://docs.rs/struct.DocumentSymbol.html)- Symbol
- A (possibly nested) symbol in a document’s outline.
- [File](https://docs.rs/struct.FileEdit.html)- Edit
- The edits to apply to one file (non-overlapping; the client sorts and applies them).
- [FileId](https://docs.rs/struct.FileId.html)
- An opaque file handle. The host owns the `FileId`→ text mapping; the library never reads paths.
- [File](https://docs.rs/struct.FilePosition.html)- Position
- A `(file, byte offset)`cursor position.
- [File](https://docs.rs/struct.FileRange.html)- Range
- A (file, range) pair — the atom of cross-file navigation results.
- [Fold](https://docs.rs/struct.FoldRange.html)- Range
- A foldable range.
- [Hover](https://docs.rs/struct.HoverResult.html)- Result
- The result of a hover query: an inferred type / signature label plus engine docs.
- [Inlay](https://docs.rs/struct.InlayHint.html)- Hint
- An inline hint rendered at a byte offset (e.g. the `: int`the engine LSP omits).
- [LineCol](https://docs.rs/struct.LineCol.html)
- A 0-based `(line, column)`position.`col`is a byte offset within the line.
- [Line](https://docs.rs/struct.LineIndex.html)- Index
- Maps byte offsets to/from `(line, column)`and UTF-16 columns.
- [NavTarget](https://docs.rs/struct.NavTarget.html)
- A navigation target (goto-definition / -declaration). Phase 2 only ever points within the same file; cross-file targets arrive in Phase 3.
- [Param](https://docs.rs/struct.ParamInfo.html)- Info
- One parameter within a `SignatureInfo`
- [Reference](https://docs.rs/struct.Reference.html)
- One reference to a symbol (find-references result), including its declaration.
- [Semantic](https://docs.rs/struct.SemanticToken.html)- Token
- A semantic-highlighting token: a source range classified by its contextual/resolved role. Drives
`textDocument/semanticTokens`— intelligence a grammar can’t produce. Modifiers are a bitset of`semantic_token_modifier`
- [Signature](https://docs.rs/struct.SignatureHelp.html)- Help
- The result of a signature-help query at a call site.
- [Signature](https://docs.rs/struct.SignatureInfo.html)- Info
- One signature shown in signature help (GDScript has no overloads, so usually one).
- [Source](https://docs.rs/struct.SourceChange.html)- Change
- A set of edits across one or more files (a cross-file rename, a quick-fix). Phase 3’s rename
spans files, so this is multi-file; a single-file change is just one `FileEdit`
- [Text](https://docs.rs/struct.TextEdit.html)- Edit
- A single text edit: replace `range`with`new_text`.
- [Text](https://docs.rs/struct.TextRange.html)- Range
- A half-open byte range `[start, end)`into a file’s UTF-8 source.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Completion](https://docs.rs/enum.CompletionKind.html)- Kind
- The kind of a completion item.
- [Diagnostic](https://docs.rs/enum.DiagnosticSource.html)- Source
- What analysis layer produced a diagnostic — lets clients group/filter parse vs. type
diagnostics without parsing the `code`.
- [Fold](https://docs.rs/enum.FoldKind.html)- Kind
- What a fold range corresponds to.
- [Inlay](https://docs.rs/enum.InlayHintKind.html)- Hint - Kind
- What an `InlayHint`
- [Reference](https://docs.rs/enum.ReferenceKind.html)- Kind
- Why a token is a reference (rust-analyzer’s `ReferenceCategory`, trimmed).
- [Rename](https://docs.rs/enum.RenameError.html)- Error
- Why a [rename](https://docs.rs/index.html)was refused — the “correct or it refuses” contract. Never a partial edit.
- [Semantic](https://docs.rs/enum.SemanticTokenType.html)- Token - Type
- The semantic role of a `SemanticToken`
- [Severity](https://docs.rs/enum.Severity.html)
- Diagnostic severity.
- [Symbol](https://docs.rs/enum.SymbolKind.html)- Kind
- The kind of a document symbol (a subset of LSP `SymbolKind`, named for GDScript).

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Cancellable](https://docs.rs/type.Cancellable.html)
- The result of a cancellable read query.
- [Markdown](https://docs.rs/type.Markdown.html)
- Documentation rendered as Markdown (engine `BBCode`already converted at codegen time).

# awsm_renderer_materials - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/awsm-renderer-materials/0.14.0/awsm_renderer_materials/

## Expand description

Pluggable material shaders for the `awsm-renderer` visibility-buffer pipeline.

See `README.md` for a high-level overview, the trait contract, and the
rationale for the askama-substitution mechanism.

Each material is a Cargo feature in this crate (`pbr-standard`, `unlit`,
`toon`). The `MaterialShader` trait is the contract every shading model
satisfies. `awsm-renderer` walks the enabled set as a registry to generate
the dispatch table and concatenate WGSL fragments at shader-template time.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use alpha_mode::`- [MaterialAlphaMode](https://docs.rs/alpha_mode/enum.MaterialAlphaMode.html);
- `pub use shader::`- [MaterialShader](https://docs.rs/shader/trait.MaterialShader.html);
- `pub use shader_id::`- [MaterialShaderId](https://docs.rs/shader_id/struct.MaterialShaderId.html);
- `pub use shader_includes::`- [FragmentInputs](https://docs.rs/shader_includes/struct.FragmentInputs.html);
- `pub use shader_includes::`- [ShaderIncludes](https://docs.rs/shader_includes/struct.ShaderIncludes.html);
- `pub use texture::`- [MaterialTexture](https://docs.rs/texture/struct.MaterialTexture.html);
- `pub use texture_context::`- [TextureContext](https://docs.rs/texture_context/trait.TextureContext.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [alpha_](https://docs.rs/alpha_mode/index.html)- mode
- Alpha mode for materials.
- [dynamic](https://docs.rs/dynamic/index.html)
- Generic dynamic-material interpreter.
- [dynamic_](https://docs.rs/dynamic_layout/index.html)- layout
- WGSL layout + packing helpers shared by `DynamicMaterial`
- [flipbook](https://docs.rs/flipbook/index.html)
- Sprite-sheet flipbook material — grid-uniform atlas, sequential cell
playback driven by `frame_globals.time`.
- [pbr](https://docs.rs/pbr/index.html)
- Physically based rendering (PBR) material parameters and packing.
- [registry](https://docs.rs/registry/index.html)
- Registry of enabled materials.
- [shader](https://docs.rs/shader/index.html)
- The `MaterialShader`trait — the public ABI of every shading model.
- [shader_](https://docs.rs/shader_id/index.html)- id
- Material shader identifiers.
- [shader_](https://docs.rs/shader_includes/index.html)- includes
- Per-material declaration of which shared shader modules and pre-shade fragment inputs a shading model needs — the heart of “skinny materials”.
- [texture](https://docs.rs/texture/index.html)
- Texture reference used by materials.
- [texture_](https://docs.rs/texture_context/index.html)- context
- Abstraction over the renderer’s texture pool / sampler set for material uniform-buffer writers.
- [toon](https://docs.rs/toon/index.html)
- Toon material — banded diffuse + stepped Blinn-Phong specular + rim.
- [unlit](https://docs.rs/unlit/index.html)
- Unlit material — constant emissive surface, no lighting.
- [writer](https://docs.rs/writer/index.html)
- Helpers for packing material parameters into the GPU storage buffer
`awsm-renderer`dispatches against.

- Worker-safe global picker for `renderer-core`.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [MAX_](https://docs.rs/constant.MAX_GPU_BUFFER_BYTES.html)- GPU_ - BUFFER_ - BYTES
- Always-on hard ceiling for a single GPU buffer allocation. A request at or
above this is rejected as a recoverable `Err`*before*it reaches the WebGPU API, instead of being passed through to abort the whole renderer process.
- [OVERSIZED_](https://docs.rs/constant.OVERSIZED_ALLOC_BYTES.html)- ALLOC_ - BYTES
- Soft diagnostic threshold: any single GPU allocation larger than this is
flagged as a likely runaway size computation (overflow / flipped count) and
logged + `debug_assert!`ed at our call site. The allocation still proceeds — this only surfaces “getting suspiciously big” early in dev. 512 MB is far past any legitimate single buffer in this renderer. Only consulted under`debug_assertions`/ the`harden-diag`feature. See`MAX_GPU_BUFFER_BYTES`

# ailake_store - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ailake-store/0.1.1/ailake_store/

## Expand description

ailake-store — object storage abstraction

Thin wrapper over object_store crate. The get_range method is critical for partial S3 reads of the HNSW footer.

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick start

Use `store_from_url` for env-based auth, or the typed builders for explicit credentials:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// URL-based (env credentials)
let store = ailake_store::store_from_url("s3://my-bucket/warehouse/my_table")?;
// Explicit static credentials (dev / CI)
use ailake_store::s3::{s3_store, S3Config, S3Credentials};
let store = s3_store(S3Config {
    bucket: "my-bucket".into(),
    region: "us-east-1".into(),
    endpoint: None,
    allow_http: false,
    credentials: S3Credentials::Static {
        access_key_id: "AKIA...".into(),
        secret_access_key: "secret".into(),
        session_token: None,
    },
}, "warehouse/my_table/")?;
```
## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use from_url::`- [store_from_url](https://docs.rs/from_url/fn.store_from_url.html);
- `pub use local::`- [LocalStore](https://docs.rs/local/struct.LocalStore.html);
- `pub use object_store_backend::`- [ObjectStoreBackend](https://docs.rs/object_store_backend/struct.ObjectStoreBackend.html);
- `pub use store::`- [Store](https://docs.rs/store/trait.Store.html);

# awsm_renderer_scene - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/awsm-renderer-scene/0.14.0/awsm_renderer_scene/

## Expand description

`awsm-renderer-scene` — the lean, canonical **runtime** scene schema for the
awsm-renderer player: a [ Scene](https://docs.rs/scene/struct.Scene.html) (

`scene.toml`) + an `assets/` directory,
all by-id. The player and renderer touch only this crate.Authoring lives elsewhere: the modifier stack + per-vertex overrides + the
editor’s `Mesh = base + edits` are in `awsm-renderer-meshgen` (recipe types) and
`awsm-renderer-editor-protocol` (the `EditorProject` document + `EditorCommand`/
`EditorQuery`), which depend on this crate and reuse its core types. The
editor’s bake step lowers authoring → runtime (`MeshDef` → [`mesh::MeshBlob`]).

Coordinate convention: right-handed, Y-up, meters. Rotations are unit
quaternions stored as `[x, y, z, w]`.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use`- [animation](https://docs.rs/animation/index.html)::*;
- `pub use`- [assets](https://docs.rs/assets/index.html)::*;
- `pub use`- [camera](https://docs.rs/camera/index.html)::*;
- `pub use`- [collider](https://docs.rs/collider/index.html)::*;
- `pub use`- [curve](https://docs.rs/curve/index.html)::*;
- `pub use`- [decal](https://docs.rs/decal/index.html)::*;
- `pub use`- [dynamic_material](https://docs.rs/dynamic_material/index.html)::*;
- `pub use`- [environment](https://docs.rs/environment/index.html)::*;
- `pub use`- [instances](https://docs.rs/instances/index.html)::*;
- `pub use`- [light](https://docs.rs/light/index.html)::*;
- `pub use`- [line](https://docs.rs/line/index.html)::*;
- `pub use`- [material](https://docs.rs/material/index.html)::*;
- `pub use`- [mesh](https://docs.rs/mesh/index.html)::*;
- `pub use`- [particle](https://docs.rs/particle/index.html)::*;
- `pub use`- [post_process](https://docs.rs/post_process/index.html)::*;
- `pub use`- [primitive](https://docs.rs/primitive/index.html)::*;
- `pub use`- [project_dir](https://docs.rs/project_dir/index.html)::*;
- `pub use`- [scene](https://docs.rs/scene/index.html)::*;
- `pub use`- [shadows](https://docs.rs/shadows/index.html)::*;
- `pub use`- [sprite](https://docs.rs/sprite/index.html)::*;
- `pub use`- [transform](https://docs.rs/transform/index.html)::*;
- `pub use`- [tree](https://docs.rs/tree/index.html)::*;

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [animation](https://docs.rs/animation/index.html)
- Persisted **animation clip**schema — the serde projection of the editor’s authored animation model (Animation mode), mirroring [`crate::StoredMaterial`].
- [assets](https://docs.rs/assets/index.html)
- Project asset table.
- [camera](https://docs.rs/camera/index.html)
- Editor-authored camera configuration.
- [collider](https://docs.rs/collider/index.html)
- [curve](https://docs.rs/curve/index.html)
- Authored 3D curves: control points + closed flag + tension + sample count.
- [decal](https://docs.rs/decal/index.html)
- Authored decal configuration. The runtime equivalent lives in
`awsm_renderer::decals::Decal`; the editor’s renderer bridge resolves the texture ref and pushes a runtime decal via`AwsmRenderer::insert_decal`.
- [dynamic_](https://docs.rs/dynamic_material/index.html)- material
- On-disk shape of a runtime-registered “custom” material.
- [environment](https://docs.rs/environment/index.html)
- [instances](https://docs.rs/instances/index.html)
- Instance-along-curve schema: place copies of a source node along a curve.
- [light](https://docs.rs/light/index.html)
- [line](https://docs.rs/line/index.html)
- Authored polylines.
- [material](https://docs.rs/material/index.html)
- Material asset (authorable PBR knobs + texture refs).
- [mesh](https://docs.rs/mesh/index.html)
- The runtime mesh — what `AssetSource::Mesh`resolves to in a baked`Scene`
- [particle](https://docs.rs/particle/index.html)
- Authored particle emitter definitions.
- [post_](https://docs.rs/post_process/index.html)- process
- Renderer-wide post-processing settings serialized into the project + player bundle.
- [primitive](https://docs.rs/primitive/index.html)
- Procedural primitive shapes — the `MeshBase::Primitive``ModifierStack``NodeKind::Mesh`backed by a`MeshDef`stack; a box/sphere/… is just a stack whose base is one of these shapes, evaluated to triangles via`awsm-renderer-meshgen`’s primitive generators.
- [project_](https://docs.rs/project_dir/index.html)- dir
- The runtime **project directory**: a`scene.toml`+ an`assets/`directory — the lean, canonical on-disk form the player loads. The editor’s bake produces one; this module owns the`scene.toml`(de)serialization + the directory layout convention.
- [scene](https://docs.rs/scene/index.html)
- The runtime scene document — the lean, canonical thing the player loads
(`scene.toml`+ an`assets/`directory). The editor authors a richer`EditorProject`(in`awsm-renderer-editor-protocol`); its**bake**step lowers that to a`Scene`
- [shadows](https://docs.rs/shadows/index.html)
- Renderer-wide shadow settings serialized into `EditorProject`.
- [sprite](https://docs.rs/sprite/index.html)
- Authored sprite / billboard nodes.
- [transform](https://docs.rs/transform/index.html)
- [tree](https://docs.rs/tree/index.html)

# futures_timer - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/futures-timer/3.0.4/target-redirect/futures_timer/

## Expand description

A general purpose crate for working with timeouts and delays with futures.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use std::time::Duration;
use futures_timer::Delay;
let now = Delay::new(Duration::from_secs(3)).await;
println!("waited for 3 secs");
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Delay](https://docs.rs/struct.Delay.html)
- A future representing the notification that an elapsed duration has occurred.

# Delay in futures_timer - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/futures-timer/3.0.4/futures_timer/struct.Delay.html

`pub struct Delay { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A future representing the notification that an elapsed duration has occurred.

This is created through the `Delay::new` method indicating when the future should fire.
Note that these futures are not intended for high resolution timers, but rather they will
likely fire some granularity after the exact instant that they’re otherwise indicated to fire
at.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

# futures_timer - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/futures-timer/latest/futures_timer/

## Expand description

A general purpose crate for working with timeouts and delays with futures.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use std::time::Duration;
use futures_timer::Delay;
let now = Delay::new(Duration::from_secs(3)).await;
println!("waited for 3 secs");
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Delay](https://docs.rs/struct.Delay.html)
- A future representing the notification that an elapsed duration has occurred.

All the builds on docs.rs are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The limits for this crate are the following:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                    If a build fails because it hit one of those limits please
                    [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                    to get them increased.

# async-std 1.13.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/async-std/^1.13

`async-std` has been discontinued; use `smol` instead

We created `async-std` to demonstrate the value of making a library as close to
`std` as possible, but async. We think that demonstration was successful, and
we hope it will influence future design and development directions of async in
`std`. However, in the meantime, the [ smol](https://github.com/smol-rs/smol/)
project came about and provided a great executor and libraries for asynchronous
use in the Rust ecosystem. We think that resources would be better spent
consolidating around

`smol`, rather than continuing to provide occasional
maintenance of `async-std`. As such, we recommend that all users of
`async-std`, and all libraries built on `async-std`, switch to `smol` instead.In addition to the `smol` project as a direct replacement, you may find other
parts of the futures ecosystem useful, including `futures-concurrency`,
`async-io`, `futures-lite`, and `async-compat`.

This crate provides an async version of [ std](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/index.html). It provides all the interfaces
you are used to, but in an async version and ready for Rust's

`async`/`await`
syntax.## Features

- **Modern:**Built from the ground up for- `std::future`and- `async/await`with blazing fast compilation time.
- **Fast:**Our robust allocator and threadpool designs provide ultra-high throughput with predictably low latency.
- **Intuitive:**Complete parity with the stdlib means you only need to learn APIs once.
- **Clear:**- [Detailed documentation](https://docs.rs/async-std)and- [accessible guides](https://book.async.rs)mean using async Rust was never easier.

## Examples

```
use task;
async
```
More examples, including networking and file access, can be found in our
[ examples](https://github.com/async-rs/async-std/tree/HEAD/examples) directory and in our

[documentation](https://docs.rs/async-std#examples).

## Philosophy

We believe Async Rust should be as easy to pick up as Sync Rust. We also believe that the best API is the one you already know. And finally, we believe that providing an asynchronous counterpart to the standard library is the best way stdlib provides a reliable basis for both performance and productivity.

Async-std is the embodiment of that vision. It combines single-allocation task creation, with an adaptive lock-free executor, threadpool and network driver to create a smooth system that processes work at a high pace with low latency, using Rust's familiar stdlib API.

---

# futures 0.3.32 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/futures/^0.3.1

`futures-rs` is a library providing the foundations for asynchronous programming in Rust.
It includes key trait definitions like `Stream`, as well as utilities like `join!`,
`select!`, and various futures combinator methods which enable expressive asynchronous
control flow.

## Usage

Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.3"
```
The current `futures` requires Rust 1.71 or later.

### Feature `std`

Futures-rs works without the standard library, such as in bare metal environments.
However, it has a significantly reduced API surface. To use futures-rs in
a `#[no_std]` environment, use:

```
[]
 = {  = "0.3",  = false }
```

# gloo-timers 0.4.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/gloo-timers/^0.4.0

Built with 🦀🕸 by The Rust and WebAssembly Working Group

Working with timers on the Web: `setTimeout` and `setInterval`.

These APIs come in two flavors:

- a callback style (that more directly mimics the JavaScript APIs), and
- a `Future`s and`Stream`s API.

### Timeouts

Timeouts fire once after a period of time (measured in milliseconds).

#### Timeouts with a Callback Function

```
use Timeout;
let timeout = new;
// Since we don't plan on cancelling the timeout, call `forget`.
timeout.forget;
```
#### Timeouts as `Future`s

With the `futures` feature enabled, a `future` module containing futures-based
timers is exposed.

# send_wrapper 0.6.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/send_wrapper/^0.6.0

# SendWrapper

This [Rust](https://www.rust-lang.org) crate implements a wrapper type called `SendWrapper` which allows you to move around non-[ Send](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/marker/trait.Send.html) types
between threads, as long as you access the contained value only from within the original thread. You also have to
make sure that the wrapper is dropped from within the original thread. If any of these constraints is violated,
a panic occurs.

The idea for this crate was born in the context of a [ GTK+](https://www.gtk.org/)/

[-based application.](http://gtk-rs.org/)

`gtk-rs`[applications are strictly single-threaded. It is not allowed to call any](https://www.gtk.org/)

`GTK+`[method from a thread different to the main thread. Consequently, all](https://www.gtk.org/)

`GTK+`[structs are non-](http://gtk-rs.org/)

`gtk-rs`[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/marker/trait.Send.html)

`Send`Sometimes you still want to do some work in background. It is possible to enqueue [ GTK+](https://www.gtk.org/) calls from there to be
executed in the main thread

[using](http://gtk-rs.org/docs/glib/source/fn.idle_add.html). This way you can know, that the

`Glib`[structs involved are only accessed in the main thread and will also be dropped there. This crate makes it possible for](http://gtk-rs.org/)

`gtk-rs`[structs to leave the main thread.](http://gtk-rs.org/)

`gtk-rs`# Examples

```
use SendWrapper;
use Rc;
use thread;
use channel;
// This import is important. It allows you to unwrap the value using deref(),
// deref_mut() or Deref coercion.
use ;
// Rc is a non-Send type.
let value = new;
// We now wrap the value with `SendWrapper` (value is moved inside).
let wrapped_value = new;
// A channel allows us to move the wrapped value between threads.
let  = channel;
let t = spawn;
let wrapped_value = receiver.recv.unwrap;
// Now you can use the value again.
let value = wrapped_value.deref;
// alternatives for dereferencing:
// let value = *wrapped_value;
// let value: &NonSendType = &wrapped_value;
// alternatives for mutable dereferencing (value and wrapped_value must be mutable too, then):
// let mut value = wrapped_value.deref_mut();
// let mut value = &mut *wrapped_value;
// let mut value: &mut NonSendType = &mut wrapped_value;
```
## Wrapping `Future`s and `Stream`s

To use `SendWrapper` on `Future`s or `Stream`s, you should enable the Cargo feature `futures` first:

```
 = {  = "0.5",  = ["futures"] }
```
Then, you can transparently wrap your `Future` or `Stream`:

```
use ;
use SendWrapper;
// `Rc` is a `!Send` type,
let value = new;
// so this `Future` is `!Send` too as increments `Rc`'s inner counter.
let future = lazy;
// We now wrap the `future` with `SendWrapper` (value is moved inside),
let wrapped_future = new;
// so now it's `Send` + `Sync` (`BoxFuture` trait object contains `Send` requirement).
let boxed_future:  = Boxpin;
let t = spawn;
```

# futures-timer 0.5.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/futures-timer/0.5.0

# futures-timer

A library for working with timers, timeouts, and intervals with the `futures`
crate.

```
# Cargo.toml
[]
 = "0.3"
```
An example of using a `Delay` is:

```
use Duration;
use *;
use Delay;
async
```
And using an `Interval`:

```
use Duration;
use *;
use Interval;
async
```
Or timing out a future

```
use Duration;
use FutureExt;
async
```

# futures-timer 0.2.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/futures-timer/0.2.1

# futures-timer

A library for working with timers, timeouts, and intervals with the `futures`
crate.

```
# Cargo.toml
[]
 = "0.1"
```
An example of using a `Delay` is:

```
use Duration;
use *;
use Delay;
async
```
And using an `Interval`:

```
use Duration;
use *;
use Interval;
async
```
Or timing out a future

```
use Duration;
use FutureExt;
async
```

# futures-timer

# futures-timer 0.1.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/futures-timer/0.1.1

# futures-timer

A library for working with timers, timeouts, and intervals with the `futures`
crate.

```
# Cargo.toml
[]
 = "0.1"
```
An example of using a `Delay` is:

```
extern crate futures;
extern crate futures_timer;
use Duration;
use *;
use Delay;
```
And using an `Interval`:

```
extern crate futures;
extern crate futures_timer;
use Duration;
use *;
use Interval;
```
Or timing out a future

```
extern crate futures_timer;
use Duration;
use FutureExt;
```

# futures-timer

A library for working with timers, timeouts, and intervals with the `futures`
crate.

```
# Cargo.toml
[]
 = "0.1"
```
An example of using a `Delay` is:

```
extern crate futures;
extern crate futures_timer;
use Duration;
use *;
use Delay;
```
And using an `Interval`:

```
extern crate futures;
extern crate futures_timer;
use Duration;
use *;
use Interval;
```

# async-std 1.13.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/async-std/1.13.2

`async-std` has been discontinued; use `smol` instead

We created `async-std` to demonstrate the value of making a library as close to
`std` as possible, but async. We think that demonstration was successful, and
we hope it will influence future design and development directions of async in
`std`. However, in the meantime, the [ smol](https://github.com/smol-rs/smol/)
project came about and provided a great executor and libraries for asynchronous
use in the Rust ecosystem. We think that resources would be better spent
consolidating around

`smol`, rather than continuing to provide occasional
maintenance of `async-std`. As such, we recommend that all users of
`async-std`, and all libraries built on `async-std`, switch to `smol` instead.In addition to the `smol` project as a direct replacement, you may find other
parts of the futures ecosystem useful, including `futures-concurrency`,
`async-io`, `futures-lite`, and `async-compat`.

This crate provides an async version of [ std](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/index.html). It provides all the interfaces
you are used to, but in an async version and ready for Rust's

`async`/`await`
syntax.## Features

- **Modern:**Built from the ground up for- `std::future`and- `async/await`with blazing fast compilation time.
- **Fast:**Our robust allocator and threadpool designs provide ultra-high throughput with predictably low latency.
- **Intuitive:**Complete parity with the stdlib means you only need to learn APIs once.
- **Clear:**- [Detailed documentation](https://docs.rs/async-std)and- [accessible guides](https://book.async.rs)mean using async Rust was never easier.

## Examples

```
use task;
async
```
More examples, including networking and file access, can be found in our
[ examples](https://github.com/async-rs/async-std/tree/HEAD/examples) directory and in our

[documentation](https://docs.rs/async-std#examples).

## Philosophy

We believe Async Rust should be as easy to pick up as Sync Rust. We also believe that the best API is the one you already know. And finally, we believe that providing an asynchronous counterpart to the standard library is the best way stdlib provides a reliable basis for both performance and productivity.

Async-std is the embodiment of that vision. It combines single-allocation task creation, with an adaptive lock-free executor, threadpool and network driver to create a smooth system that processes work at a high pace with low latency, using Rust's familiar stdlib API.

---
